children.text: At zero temperature superfluid helium is incompressible with density \(\rho\). Its flow is irrotational except along thin vortex filaments of core radius \(a\). A closed path linking one filament has circulation \(\pm2\pi\kappa\), where \(\kappa=\hbar/m_{He}\). A contractible path has zero circulation. Velocity fields superpose like magnetic fields of current-carrying wires, and each filament moves with the local flow due to the other filaments. Neglect the core contribution to energy and assume all relevant logarithms are large. A circular vortex loop of radius R has energy \(U\simeq2\pi^2\rho\kappa^2R\ln(R/a)\) and momentum \(P=2\pi^2\rho\kappa R^2\), normal to its plane by the circulation right-hand rule. In all questions draw directions as well as giving requested magnitudes. Solid walls impose zero normal flow.

statement.text:
Vortices in Superfluid
At zero temperature superfluid helium is incompressible with density \(\rho\). Its flow is irrotational except along thin vortex filaments of core radius \(a\). A closed path linking one filament has circulation \(\pm2\pi\kappa\), where \(\kappa=\hbar/m_{He}\). A contractible path has zero circulation. Velocity fields superpose like magnetic fields of current-carrying wires, and each filament moves with the local flow due to the other filaments. Neglect the core contribution to energy and assume all relevant logarithms are large. A circular vortex loop of radius R has energy \(U\simeq2\pi^2\rho\kappa^2R\ln(R/a)\) and momentum \(P=2\pi^2\rho\kappa R^2\), normal to its plane by the circulation right-hand rule. In all questions draw directions as well as giving requested magnitudes. Solid walls impose zero normal flow.

A.1. Straight-filament flow

A straight vertical vortex lies on the axis of a beaker of radius \(R_0\gg a\). Draw streamlines and find velocity at radius r.
A.2. Single-vortex surface
Find the free-surface height profile, neglecting surface tension.
B.1. Equal-circulation pair


Two identical straight vortices are initially separated by \(r_0\). Find their initial velocities and trajectories.
B.2. Lattice trajectories

A beaker contains a triangular lattice of identical vortices with spacing \(u\ll R_0\). Draw the trajectories of A, B and the central vortex C.
B.3. Lattice velocity
Find the coarse-grained speed of a vortex at radial distance r.
B.4. Lattice spacing in time
Find \(AB(t)\), given \(AB(0)\).
B.5. Smoothed lattice surface
Find the free surface after smoothing out individual vortex cores.
C.1. Rectangular-loop momentum


A nearly rectangular vortex loop has dimensions \(b\times d\), with \(a\ll b\ll d\). Find momentum and its direction.
C.2. Rectangular-loop energy
Find its leading-logarithm energy.
C.3. Shifted-filament momentum

A filament of length d shifts by b along x. Find the change of fluid momentum and its direction.
D.1. Charged straight filament

A straight vortex has charge per length \(\lambda<0\) and is placed in uniform transverse electric field E. Find trajectory and velocity.
D.2. Charged-ring radius

A circular loop initially has radius \(R_0\) and uniform linear charge \(\lambda<0\). Uniform E is normal to its plane and opposite its initial momentum. Draw the centre path and find R(t).
D.3. Charged-ring velocity
Find the loop speed as a function of time in the leading-logarithm approximation.
D.4. Field switched off
At time \(t_*\), E is switched off and speed is \(v_*\). Find later speed.
E.1. One flat wall

A straight vortex is initially distance \(h_0\) from a flat impermeable wall. Draw its trajectory and find its velocity.
E.2. Right-angle corner

A straight vortex is distance \(h_0\) from each of two perpendicular walls. Find its initial velocity.
E.3. Corner trajectory
Draw the vortex trajectory and direction.
E.4. Long-time corner speed
Find the speed after a long time.

children.text: Symmetry gives concentric circles. Circulation \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\) implies \(v=\kappa/r\), directed according to the circulation.
The free-surface slope obeys \(g\,dz/dr=v^2/r=\kappa^2/r^3\). Integrating, \[z(r)=z_0-\kappa^2/(2gr^2).\] The constant follows from liquid volume and the formula excludes the core.

Each moves at \(\kappa/r_0\) perpendicular to their connecting line. They orbit their midpoint on opposite semicircles of radius \(r_0/2\), with common angular speed \(2\kappa/r_0^2\). By contrast, opposite-circulation vortices translate together.
The coarse-grained lattice rotates rigidly. A and B trace circles about the beaker centre. The central vortex C stays at the centre.
The number per area is \(2/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Summing circulation inside a circle gives \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\pi r^2\,2/(\sqrt3u^2)\), so \[v=2\pi\kappa r/(\sqrt3u^2).\]
The angular velocity \(2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\) is independent of radius. Rigid rotation preserves separation: \(AB(t)=AB(0)\).
Rigid-body angular speed is \(\Omega=2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Integrating \(g\,dz/dr=\Omega^2r\) gives \[z=z_0+2\pi^2\kappa^2r^2/(3gu^4).\]
Circulation times oriented area times density gives \(P=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), normal to the loop by the circulation right-hand rule.

The two long opposite filaments each contribute kinetic energy. Integrating from core a to separation b, or using the two-wire inductance analogue, gives \[U=2\pi\rho\kappa^2d\ln(b/a).\] End corrections are smaller for \(b\ll d\).

The difference between old and new flow is the flow of a rectangular loop. Thus \(|\Delta P|=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), perpendicular to both the filament and its displacement. Its sign is fixed by the oriented loop formed by the new filament and the negative old filament.

For length d, electric force is \(\lambda d\mathbf E\). Momentum changes perpendicular to filament displacement, so the constant drift is perpendicular to E, with magnitude \(|\lambda|E/(2\pi\kappa\rho)\). Choose the sign using C.3. The path is a straight line, with no ordinary mass-times-acceleration law for the vortex.

Total charge is fixed at \(-2\pi R_0|\lambda|\), so force is constant and parallel to initial momentum. From \(P=P_0+2\pi ER_0|\lambda|t\), \[R(t)=\sqrt{R_0^2+ER_0|\lambda|t/(\pi\rho\kappa)}.\] The centre moves along the ring axis in the force direction. Charge density decreases as the ring grows.

Work and momentum balance imply \(v=dU/dP\). With the given U and P, \[v\simeq\frac{\kappa}{2R(t)}\ln\frac{R(t)}a.\] Differentiating the approximate energy exactly adds a 1 inside the logarithmic bracket, which is beyond leading-logarithm accuracy. As R grows the speed decreases in the large-log regime. Replacing the slowly varying logarithm by \(\ln(R_0/a)\) gives the further approximation in the source.
With no external force momentum stays constant, hence radius and speed stay constant: \(v(t)=v_*\) for \(t>t_*\).

An opposite-circulation image across the wall enforces zero normal flow. Its distance is \(2h_0\). The vortex translates parallel to the wall at constant speed \(\kappa/(2h_0)\), with direction fixed by the image circulation.

Use three images: opposite circulation across each wall and equal circulation across both. At \((h_0,h_0)\) the net components are opposite with magnitudes \(\kappa/(4h_0)\). The speed is \(\kappa/(2\sqrt2h_0)\), tangent to the corner trajectory.

Energy conservation for the four-image arrangement implies \[(x^2+y^2)/(x^2y^2)=2/h_0^2.\] The curve passes through \((h_0,h_0)\), tangent to the direction with opposite x and y components. It approaches one wall at a fixed distance as it travels far along it, with direction set by the circulation.
For \(x\to\infty\), the trajectory invariant yields \(y\to h_0/\sqrt2\). Only the nearest-wall image matters, giving \[v_\infty=\kappa/(2y)=\kappa/(\sqrt2h_0).\]

Vortices in Superfluid
A.1. Straight-filament flow
Symmetry gives concentric circles. Circulation \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\) implies \(v=\kappa/r\), directed according to the circulation.
A.2. Single-vortex surface
The free-surface slope obeys \(g\,dz/dr=v^2/r=\kappa^2/r^3\). Integrating, \[z(r)=z_0-\kappa^2/(2gr^2).\] The constant follows from liquid volume and the formula excludes the core.

B.2. Lattice trajectories
The coarse-grained lattice rotates rigidly. A and B trace circles about the beaker centre. The central vortex C stays at the centre.
B.3. Lattice velocity
The number per area is \(2/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Summing circulation inside a circle gives \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\pi r^2\,2/(\sqrt3u^2)\), so \[v=2\pi\kappa r/(\sqrt3u^2).\]
B.4. Lattice spacing in time
The angular velocity \(2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\) is independent of radius. Rigid rotation preserves separation: \(AB(t)=AB(0)\).
B.5. Smoothed lattice surface
Rigid-body angular speed is \(\Omega=2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Integrating \(g\,dz/dr=\Omega^2r\) gives \[z=z_0+2\pi^2\kappa^2r^2/(3gu^4).\]
C.1. Rectangular-loop momentum
Circulation times oriented area times density gives \(P=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), normal to the loop by the circulation right-hand rule.
C.2. Rectangular-loop energy
The two long opposite filaments each contribute kinetic energy. Integrating from core a to separation b, or using the two-wire inductance analogue, gives \[U=2\pi\rho\kappa^2d\ln(b/a).\] End corrections are smaller for \(b\ll d\).
C.3. Shifted-filament momentum
The difference between old and new flow is the flow of a rectangular loop. Thus \(|\Delta P|=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), perpendicular to both the filament and its displacement. Its sign is fixed by the oriented loop formed by the new filament and the negative old filament.
D.1. Charged straight filament

D.2. Charged-ring radius

An opposite-circulation image across the wall enforces zero normal flow. Its distance is \(2h_0\). The vortex translates parallel to the wall at constant speed \(\kappa/(2h_0)\), with direction fixed by the image circulation.
E.2. Right-angle corner
